Xin had known Wei since university in Vancouver, so she could read the weather in him. In October he was almost his old self at her birthday dinner, teasing Lan about her terrible karaoke, holding her hand under the table.
Two weeks later a letter from the bank came to their old address, and at midnight he texted Xin: "Just when I thought it was over." That weekend he was polite with Lan, careful, far away.
November was good again. Mostly.
Over dumplings, Wei admitted he hated the bad days. "I think I've forgiven her, and then my chest remembers."
Xin didn't tell him to hurry up. She said the good weeks counted too. Then, gently: "If it keeps catching you like this, a counsellor might help you two talk about it without ripping it open every time."
Wei nodded slowly and wrote down a name on his napkin.

qa.q: Where had Xin known Wei since?
qa.a: Xin had known Wei since university in Vancouver.

qa.q: What does Wei mean when he says 'my chest remembers'?
qa.a: Wei feels he has forgiven Lan in his head, but the hurt still flares when something like the bank letter brings the memory back.

qa.q: How did Xin support Wei in a helpful way?
qa.a: Xin was patient, reminded Wei that the good weeks counted, and suggested a counsellor so the couple could talk without reopening the wound each time. 🤍

qa.q: How might Lan experience the distant weekend after the letter?
qa.a: Lan probably feels it as a step backwards and may worry the progress is gone, even though November shows it wasn't.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that trust returns unevenly, with good weeks and flare-ups, and suggesting a counsellor if the hurt will not ease.

The staff canteen at the district hospital is loud at one o'clock, but Nirmala, his friend since their nursing college days, could still tell when Gurpreet wasn't really listening. For a month he'd been easier: laughing at the ward jokes, showing her photos of the Sunday picnic with his wife Harleen and the kids. Today he was pushing his rajma around and not eating it.
"Bad day?" she asked.
"Harleen's cousin came by with sweets to celebrate his new shop," he said. "Just sweets. And I thought of the loan and couldn't breathe for a second. I thought we were past it."
Nirmala, who had watched him go from silent in March to smiling in June, said, "You're past a lot of it. It just comes back in waves. That's not failure."
He shrugged. "Some nights it won't let go."
"Then maybe see the counsellor on the second floor, both of you," she said. "Someone who can keep the conversation steady."

qa.q: What was Gurpreet doing with his rajma?
qa.a: Gurpreet was pushing his rajma around and not eating it.

qa.q: Why did the cousin's visit shake Gurpreet?
qa.a: Family arriving to celebrate a new shop brought the loan back, and Gurpreet felt the old hurt so strongly he couldn't breathe for a second.

qa.q: What did Nirmala offer that could help the healing continue?
qa.a: Nirmala pointed out how far Gurpreet had come, called the setbacks waves rather than failure, and suggested the couple see a counsellor together.

qa.q: What might Harleen notice at home on a day like this?
qa.a: Harleen may see Gurpreet go quiet again and wonder if they have slipped back, even though the good weeks were real.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague observing uneven healing, with good weeks and flare-ups, and pointing toward a counsellor when the hurt will not ease.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,

Since you asked what I honestly think after staying with you both last week, here it is.

On Tuesday you and Nisha were cooking together, laughing about the burnt rotis, and I thought: they're through it. On Thursday she got a call from her brother, stepped onto the balcony to take it, and I watched your whole face close. You barely spoke through dinner.

I don't think Thursday cancels Tuesday. From outside it looks like trust coming back in fits, a good week and then a bad evening when the memory flares. That seems normal to me, even if it's exhausting from inside.

But you also told me you still wake up angry some nights, a year on. If that doesn't ease, please think about seeing a counsellor together. Not to dig it all up again, but so you two can talk about it without it turning into the same fight.

I'm around. Call me when Thursdays happen.

Ritu

qa.q: What were Jeevan and Nisha laughing about on Tuesday?
qa.a: They were laughing about the burnt rotis while cooking together.

qa.q: What does Ritu seem to feel after watching Thursday's dinner?
qa.a: Ritu feels concerned for Jeevan but also hopeful, believing the bad evening does not cancel the good week.

qa.q: What does Ritu suggest if Jeevan's anger does not ease, and why is it a wise step?
qa.a: Ritu suggests seeing a counsellor together, because a counsellor could help them talk about it without it becoming the same fight again.

qa.a: The memory flares; Jeevan may feel suspicious and hurt all over again, and Jeevan's face closes, with barely a word spoken through dinner.

passage:
You asked what it looks like when a couple gets through something like that. I'm Kiran, and I've watched Mahima and Dev closely for about a year now, so I'll tell you what I saw.

It isn't a straight line. There was a stretch in spring where they came to every dinner holding hands, finishing each other's jokes, and I honestly thought, done, healed. Then one evening Mahima's brother turned up at our place unannounced, and I watched Dev go completely still. He left early. She sat in my kitchen afterwards saying, "I thought we were past this."

They weren't, not that night. But two weeks later they were fine again.

What helped, I think, was that neither of them treated the bad days as proof it had all failed. And when the bad days kept coming back around the same things, they started seeing a counsellor. Mahima says it lets them talk without scraping the wound open again. That's what I've seen, anyway.

qa.q: Who turned up unannounced one evening?
qa.a: Mahima's brother.

qa.q: How does Kiran seem to feel when Dev goes completely still and leaves early?
qa.a: Kiran seems surprised and a little disappointed after thinking they were healed, and concerned for both of them.

qa.q: What helped Mahima and Dev keep going through the setbacks?
qa.a: They did not treat a bad day as proof that everything had failed, and when the same things kept coming back, they got help from a counsellor.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima when she says "I thought we were past this"?
qa.a: She feels hurt and discouraged, maybe a little frightened, because a good stretch suddenly slipped back.

grounding: Kiran, a friend, describes how trust between Mahima and Dev returned in uneven waves and how a counsellor helped them talk without reopening the wound.

Binita sits two desks from me at the insurance office, so I've had a front-row seat to the last few months, though I only know what she's chosen to tell me.

In January she barely ate lunch; she said things at home were "complicated" after her husband found out about a loan. By March she was showing me photos from a weekend trip they'd taken, all smiles. I thought it was over.

Then one Monday in April she came in with red eyes and said, "We had a bad day. He saw a message from my brother and it all came back."

I didn't know what to say, so I just said the good stretches probably still count.

Last week she mentioned they'd been to see a counsellor, because the bad days kept circling the same argument. She seemed lighter afterwards, or maybe I just wanted her to be.

— Avni

qa.q: What did Binita show Avni in March?
qa.a: Photos from a weekend trip they'd taken, all smiles.

qa.q: How does Avni feel watching Binita's ups and downs?
qa.a: Avni cares about Binita and feels hopeful, but is also unsure, admitting that Binita may only seem lighter because Avni wants her to be.

qa.q: Was Avni's reply on the red-eyed Monday helpful, and why?
qa.a: Yes; saying the good stretches still count was simple and kind, and it did not push Binita to explain more than she chose to.

qa.q: What is it like for Binita when a message from her brother brings it all back?
qa.a: It likely feels discouraging and painful, as if the good weeks were suddenly erased, even though they were real.

grounding: Avni, a colleague, observes Binita's marriage healing unevenly after a hidden loan, with good weeks and bad days, and notes that a counsellor helped.

March: Sudha met Damini for lunch. Damini was smiling for the first time in weeks. "Kunal and I went to the beach. He held my hand. I think we're okay." Sudha was glad, but careful not to say "so it's over."

April: Sudha stopped by with mangoes and found Damini red-eyed. A letter from the bank had come, a routine one, and Kunal had gone silent for a whole day. "I thought we'd moved past it," Damini said. Sudha sat beside her. "Maybe it's not backwards. Maybe healing is just bumpy."

June: Over coffee, Damini said the bad days were fewer, but they still came. Sudha said gently, "If it keeps flaring up, a counsellor might help you both talk about it without reopening everything." Damini nodded slowly. "Kunal said the same thing last week."

qa.q: What did Sudha bring in April?
qa.a: She brought mangoes.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she saw Damini smiling in March?
qa.a: Sudha felt glad and relieved, but also cautious, not wanting to declare the problem finished.

qa.q: What did Sudha offer that could help the couple?
qa.a: Patience with setbacks and the idea of seeing a counsellor if the hurt keeps flaring, so they can talk safely.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini when a routine bank letter sets things back?
qa.a: Damini feels discouraged and hurt, afraid their progress has been lost when the old memory flares.

grounding: Over several months a friend sees trust return unevenly, urges patience with setbacks and suggests a counsellor if the hurt does not ease.
